claim: Nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) change composition as organisms age in many species.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) mediates nearly all exchanges between nucleus and cytoplasm, and in many species, it changes composition as the organism ages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about NPCs across species.

claim: SAGA-dependent attachment of DNA circles to NPCs in replicatively ageing yeast cells causes NPCs to lose their nuclear basket and cytoplasmic complexes.
source: We show that SAGA-dependent attachment of DNA circles to NPCs in replicatively ageing yeast cells causes NPCs to lose their nuclear basket and cytoplasmic complexes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs lacking basket and cytoplasmic complexes were not recognized as defective by the NPC quality control machinery (SINC).
source: These NPCs were not recognized as defective by the NPC quality control machinery (SINC) and not targeted by ESCRTs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no recruitment of SINC/ESCRT components to circle-bound NPCs.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs were not targeted by ESCRTs.
source: These NPCs were not recognized as defective by the NPC quality control machinery (SINC) and not targeted by ESCRTs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no accumulation of ESCRT components at circle-bound NPCs.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs interacted normally or more effectively with protein import and export factors.
source: They interacted normally or more effectively with protein import and export factors but specifically lost mRNA export factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification of karyopherin localization to circle-bound NPCs.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs specifically lost mRNA export factors.
source: They interacted normally or more effectively with protein import and export factors but specifically lost mRNA export factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification showing depletion of mRNA export factors from circle-bound NPCs.

claim: Acetylation of Nup60 drove the displacement of basket and cytoplasmic complexes from circle-bound NPCs.
source: Acetylation of Nup60 drove the displacement of basket and cytoplasmic complexes from circle-bound NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that the non-acetylatable Nup60-K467R mutant retained basket and cytoplasmic components.

claim: Mutations preventing NPC remodeling extended the replicative lifespan of cells.
source: Mutations preventing this remodeling extended the replicative lifespan of the cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by lifespan analysis showing that nup60-K467R cells lived longer than wild-type.

claim: In post-mitotic cells such as neurons, core NPC components do not turnover.
source: In post-mitotic cells such as neurons, core NPC components do not turnover, tend to become oxidized over time and progressively lose functionality (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Core NPC components in post-mitotic cells tend to become oxidized over time.
source: In post-mitotic cells such as neurons, core NPC components do not turnover, tend to become oxidized over time and progressively lose functionality (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Core NPC components in post-mitotic cells progressively lose functionality.
source: In post-mitotic cells such as neurons, core NPC components do not turnover, tend to become oxidized over time and progressively lose functionality (Savas et al., 2012; Toyama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In neurons of old rats, NPCs become increasingly leaky with age, affecting proper retention of nucleoplasmic proteins in the nucleus.
source: Accordingly, in the neurons of old rats NPCs become increasingly leaky with age, affecting the proper retention of nucleoplasmic proteins in the nucleus (D'Angelo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast NPCs are targeted by a quality control machinery that removes damaged or misassembled NPCs.
source: On the opposite, yeast NPCs are targeted by a quality control machinery that removes damaged or misassembled NPCs (Webster et al., 2014; Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: No oxidized NPCs are observed in replicatively ageing yeast cells.
source: Accordingly, no oxidized NPCs are observed in replicatively ageing yeast cells (Rempel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Proteomics analysis of old yeast cells indicates they progressively change NPC composition, losing their nuclear basket and cytoplasmic complexes.
source: Still, proteomics analysis of the old yeast cells indicate that they progressively change composition, losing their nuclear basket and cytoplasmic complexes (Janssens et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous proteomics studies.

claim: Similar NPC composition changes are observed in the liver of ageing rats.
source: Similar changes are observed in the liver of ageing rats (Ori et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Replicative ageing of budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is driven by its asymmetric mode of cell division.
source: The replicative ageing of the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae is driven by its asymmetric mode of cell division, during which the larger mother cells bud daughters off their surface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: Yeast mother cells retain and accumulate diverse ageing factors.
source: These mother cells retain and accumulate diverse ageing factors (Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014; Mortimer and Johnston, 1959).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast mother cells stop dividing after generating 20-30 daughter cells and ultimately die.
source: Therefore, after generating 20–30 daughter cells they stop dividing and ultimately die.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast replicative lifespan.

claim: Retention of ageing factors in mother cells resets age and lifespan potential of their daughters.
source: Retention of the ageing factors in the mother cells resets age and lifespan potential of their daughters.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast asymmetric division.

claim: Extra-chromosomal DNA circles are prominent ageing factors at least in yeast.
source: Extra-chromosomal DNA circles are prominent ageing factors at least in yeast (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA circles are generated in virtually all mother cells at some point in their lifespan through excision of chromosomal fragments.
source: These circles are generated in virtually all mother cells at some point in their lifespan through excision of chromosomal fragments (Moller et al., 2018; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The rDNA locus is the primary source of extrachromosomal DNA circles due to its repeated nature and high copy number.
source: Due to its repeated nature and high copy number, the rDNA locus is the primary source of such circles, called extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERC formation in yeast.

claim: Non-chromosomal DNA circles are tightly retained in the mother during cell division.
source: Non-chromosomal DNA circles are tightly retained in the mother during cell division (Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Circles that contain a replication origin replicate once per division cycle and accumulate exponentially in ageing mother cells over time.
source: Circles that contain a replication origin, like ERCs, replicate once per division cycle and accumulate exponentially in ageing mother cells over time.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERC replication and accumulation.

claim: Ageing yeast cells may contain up to a thousand ERCs at the end of their life, representing about as much DNA as the rest of the genome.
source: These cells may then contain up to a thousand ERCs at the end of their life, which represents about as much DNA as the rest of the genome (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutants that form ERCs at a reduced rate, such as fob1∆ mutant cells, show an extended replicative lifespan.
source: Mutants that form ERCs at a reduced rate, such as the fob1∆ mutant cells, show an extended replicative lifespan (RLS; Defossez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Cells lacking the sirtuin Sir2 show a higher rate of ERC formation, accumulate them faster and are short-lived.
source: In reverse, cells in which recombination in the rDNA is derepressed, such as cells lacking the sirtuin Sir2, show a higher rate of ERC formation, accumulate them faster and are short-lived (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Artificially introducing an ERC or any other replicating DNA circle in young cells causes their premature ageing.
source: Finally, artificially introducing an ERC (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997) or any other replicating DNA circle in young cells (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Falcón and Aris, 2003) causes their premature ageing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Yeast cells undergo a closed mitosis with the nuclear envelope and NPCs remaining intact through mitosis.
source: Yeast cells undergo a closed mitosis, the nuclear envelope and NPCs remaining intact through mitosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: Tight retention of DNA circles in the mother cell depends on their anchorage to the nuclear periphery through NPCs.
source: Tight retention of DNA circles in the mother cell depends on their anchorage to the nuclear periphery, through NPCs (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Anchorage of DNA circles to NPCs is mediated by SAGA, a large multi-subunit complex harboring acetyl-transferase activity provided by Gcn5.
source: Anchorage is mediated by SAGA, a large multi-subunit complex harboring acetyl-transferase activity (provided by Gcn5) and which binds both chromatin (Durand et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020) and NPCs, via its subunit Sgf73 and the nucleoporin Nup1 (Jani et al., 2014; Köhler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SAGA binds both chromatin and NPCs via its subunit Sgf73 and the nucleoporin Nup1.
source: Anchorage is mediated by SAGA, a large multi-subunit complex harboring acetyl-transferase activity (provided by Gcn5) and which binds both chromatin (Durand et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020) and NPCs, via its subunit Sgf73 and the nucleoporin Nup1 (Jani et al., 2014; Köhler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ERC retention in wild type mother cells causes the accumulation of NPCs to which they are bound, such that ageing wild-type cells may contain up to 10-fold more NPCs than young ones.
source: ERC retention in wild type mother cells also causes the accumulation of the NPCs to which they are bound, such that ageing wild-type cells may contain up to 10-fold more NPCs than young ones (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutations preventing ERC formation or accumulation dampen NPC accumulation with time and extend the replicative longevity of the cell.
source: Furthermore, mutations preventing ERC formation or accumulation dampen NPC accumulation with time and extend the replicative longevity of the cell.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The yeast nuclear pore complex is a ~50 megadalton structure comprising repetitions of more than 30 different subunits called nucleoporins.
source: The yeast nuclear pore complex is a ~ 50 megadalton structure comprising repetitions of more than 30 different subunits, called nucleoporins (short Nups) (Beck and Hurt, 2016; Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The core of the NPC is inserted in the nuclear envelope and stabilized by additional protein rings on both the cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic sides of the pore.
source: The core of the NPC, also called the inner pore ring, is inserted in the nuclear envelope and stabilized by additional protein rings on both the cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic sides of the pore (Bui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: FG-Nups form a barrier to passive diffusion and facilitate the passage of transport cargos across the NPC.
source: The center is filled by so-called FG-Nups, which both form a barrier to passive diffusion and facilitate the passage of transport cargos across the NPC (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2016; Peters, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NPCs are decorated on their cytoplasmic face by a complex of cytoplasmic Nups described as fibrils or filaments.
source: On their cytoplasmic face, NPCs are decorated by a complex of cytoplasmic Nups which have been also described as fibrils or filaments (Fernandez-Martinez et al., 2016; Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The nuclear basket is formed mainly of the extended protein TPR, known as Mlp1 and Mlp2 in yeast, and anchored to NPCs by the protein Nup60.
source: On their nucleoplasmic side, they assemble the so-called nuclear basket formed mainly of the extended protein TPR, known as Mlp1 and Mlp2 in yeast (Strambio-de-Castillia et al., 1999), and anchored to NPCs by the protein Nup60.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The nuclear basket mediates NPC-chromatin interaction.
source: The basket mediates NPC-chromatin interaction (Niepel et al., 2013) and contributes to mRNA quality control and export (Green et al., 2003; Vinciguerra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclear basket contributes to mRNA quality control and export.
source: The basket mediates NPC-chromatin interaction (Niepel et al., 2013) and contributes to mRNA quality control and export (Green et al., 2003; Vinciguerra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All tested stable core Nups accumulated in the NPC cap adjacent to DNA circle clusters to similar extents, showing a 2.4-fold enrichment compared to their localization elsewhere in the nuclear envelope.
source: In these cells, all the stable core Nups, i.e., the scaffold components (outer ring: Nup84, Nup133; inner ring: Nup170, Nic96) and the components of the transport channel (FG-Nups: Nup53, Nup59) accumulated in the cap to similar extents. Quantification of their fluorescence indicated a 2.4-fold enrichment (median), compared to their localization elsewhere in the nuclear envelope (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: DNA circles bind intact NPC cores.
source: All tested core Nups showed the same enrichment in the cap, indicating that the DNA circles bind intact NPC cores.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all core Nups accumulate equally at the cap.

claim: Most peripheral subunits on both sides of the NPC did not accumulate in the cap adjacent to DNA circle clusters.
source: In striking contrast to core Nups, most peripheral subunits on both sides of the NPC did not accumulate in the cap. Four out of the five components of the nuclear basket and four out of the six components of the cytoplasmic complexes were present only at reduced levels or excluded from the cap (Figure 1C and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C and E.

claim: Only Nup1 and Nup83 with its partner Nup159 accumulated together with the core NPC at the cap.
source: Only Nup1, which appears to be more stably associated to NPCs than the other basket components (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014), and Nup83 and its partner Nup159, which form the docking site for the cytoplasmic complexes at the cytoplasmic side of NPCs, accumulated together with the core NPC.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data and citation to a previous study.

claim: The basket components Mlp1, Mlp2 and Nup60 were excluded from the NPC cap adjacent to DNA circle clusters.
source: The basket components Mlp1, Mlp2 and Nup60 seemed literally excluded from the cap (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs showed an altered stoichiometry very reminiscent of that observed for the NPCs of old yeast mother cells as estimated by Mass-spectrometry.
source: Thus, they showed an altered stoichiometry very reminiscent of that observed for the NPCs of old yeast mother cells, as estimated by Mass-spectrometry (Janssens et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous mass-spectrometry studies.

claim: Core Nups Nup159 and Nup170 colocalized similarly in young and old mother cells with average correlation of 0.78 ± 0.03 and 0.79 ± 0.02 respectively.
source: Analysis of Pearson correlation between the signals of core Nups (Nup159-mCherry and Nup170-GFP), showed that it was similarly high in young and old mother cells (average correlation = 0.78 ± 0.03, n = 33 and 0.79 ± 0.02, n = 30, respectively; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The basket proteins Nup60 and Mlp1 and the cytoplasmic protein Gle1 colocalized less extensively with the core NPC in young cells compared to core Nups.
source: In contrast, the basket proteins Nup60 and Mlp1 and the cytoplasmic protein Gle1 (fused to GFP) colocalized less extensively with the core NPC (Nup159-mCherry) already in young cells (average correlation = 0.68 ± .0.04, n = 32; 0.61 ± 0.04, n = 31 and 0.62 ± 0.05; n = 32 respectively), consistent with these proteins associating more transiently with NPCs (Denning et al., 2001; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Dilworth et al., 2001; Niepel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data and citations to previous studies.

claim: The correlation between basket/cytoplasmic proteins and core NPCs substantially dropped in old cells compared to young cells (p < 10–4).
source: Moreover, the correlation substantially dropped in old cells (average correlation 0.35 ± 0.05, n = 33; 0.31 ± 0.06, n = 37 and 0.24 ± 0.06, n = 35 respectively; p < 10–4; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In yeast mother cells that underwent unperturbed ageing, a substantial fraction of the NPCs lacks a basket and cytoplasmic complexes.
source: Thus, in yeast mother cells that underwent unperturbed ageing, a substantial fraction of the NPCs lacks a basket and cytoplasmic complexes, in line with mass-spectrometry data from old yeast cells (Janssens et al., 2015; Rempel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data and supported by citations to previous mass-spectrometry studies.

claim: Aged fob1∆ mutant cells did not show any significant dissociation of the basket from NPCs after 22-24 budding cycles compared to young cells.
source: Strikingly, unlike wild type cells of the same age, the aged fob1∆ mutant cells did not show any significant dissociation of the basket from NPCs after 22–24 budding cycles compared to young wild type and young fob1∆ mutant cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Deleting the SGF73 gene restored the localization of the basket to NPCs in aged cells.
source: Moreover, deleting the SGF73 gene, which docks SAGA to NPCs and mediates circle anchorage to nuclear pores (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014), also restored the localization of the basket to NPCs in aged cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B and citation to a previous study.

claim: ERC presence, attachment and SAGA function are required for the basket to be displaced from NPCs in old cells.
source: Thus, ERC presence, attachment and SAGA function are required for the basket to be displaced from NPCs in old cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments with fob1∆ and sgf73∆ mutants.

claim: Daughter cells of old mothers rapidly recovered the proper localization of the basket proteins.
source: Indeed, when comparing signal correlation between the basket proteins Nup60 or Mlp1, with the core Nup, Nup159, colocalization between basket and core NPCs was restored in the rejuvenated daughter cells of old mothers, to the level observed in both young mothers and their daughters (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The formation of ERCs and their attachment to NPCs drives the accumulation of basket-less NPCs in old cells.
source: We conclude that the formation of ERCs and their attachment to NPCs drives the accumulation of basket-less NPCs in old cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the experiments showing that preventing ERC formation or attachment prevents basket loss.

claim: A quality control system called SINC (Storage of Improperly assembled NPCs Compartment) recruits the ESCRT III machinery to defective NPCs and mediates their removal from the nuclear envelope.
source: This quality control system, called Storage of Improperly assembled NPCs Compartment (SINC), recruits the ESCRT III machinery, including its component Snf7, the adaptor protein Chm7 and the AAA-ATPase Vps4, to defective NPCs and mediates their removal from the nuclear envelope (Rempel et al., 2019; Webster et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neither Vps4 nor Snf7 accumulated near the circle cluster more than anywhere else in the nuclear envelope.
source: Quantification of the GFP fluorescence emitted by either of these labeled proteins at the nuclear periphery surrounding or away from the cluster (depicted in Figure 4B, as in Figure 1D) indicated that neither Vps4 nor Snf7 accumulated near the circle cluster more than anywhere else in the nuclear envelope (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chm7-GFP did not accumulate more frequently around the circle cluster than elsewhere.
source: Similarly, Chm7-GFP, an SINC marker (Webster et al., 2016), which shows a more diffuse localization but still forms several brighter dots per cell, did not accumulate more frequently around the circle cluster than elsewhere (Figure 4—figure supplement 1.).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs are not recognized as being defective by the cell.
source: Thus, we found no evidence that the the NPCs associated with the reporter DNA circle would be particularly targeted to the SINC or particularly recruit the ESCRT system, indicating circle-bound NPCs are not recognized as being defective by the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of ESCRT/SINC component accumulation at circle-bound NPCs.

claim: The amount of Net1-decorated material increased more than 10-fold in the nucleus of old mother cells compared to young ones, consistent with these cells accumulating ERCs with age.
source: As described, the amount of Net1-decorated material indeed increased more than 10-fold in the nucleus of the old mother cells compared to young ones, consistent with these cells accumulating ERCs with age (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Vps4 and Snf7 did not accumulate around or at the Net1 clusters compared to the rest of the cell in old cells.
source: However, we did not find any accumulation of these proteins immediately around or at the Net1 clusters compared to the rest of the cell (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Neither the NPCs associated with the reporter circle in young cells nor those associated with the ERCs in old cells are recognized as defective by the cell.
source: Thus, neither the NPCs associated with the reporter circle in young cells nor those associated with the ERCs in old cells are recognized as defective by the cell.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of ESCRT recruitment to both reporter circle-bound and ERC-bound NPCs.

claim: Old mother cells accumulate older NPCs over time as indicated by increased red to green signal ratio in Nup170-mCh-sfGFP (p < 0.001).
source: However, over time we also observed a highly significant increase of the red to green signal ratio in old compared to young mother cells (n = 29 old cells, p < 0.001), indicating that old cells might actually accumulate old pores over time.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of fluorescence timer data.

claim: The NPCs of daughter cells were not significantly less red-shifted in average compared to old mother cells.
source: Strikingly, the NPCs of their daughter cells were not significantly less red-shifted in average (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The composition difference of NPCs between mother and daughter cells is not driven by their age.
source: Thus, although old mother cells might accumulate older NPCs, the composition difference of these NPCs between mother and daughter cells is not driven by their age.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that daughter NPCs are not significantly younger than mother NPCs despite having different compositions.

claim: The two basket-associated proteins Esc1 and Ulp1 were excluded from NPC caps adjacent to DNA circle clusters.
source: Consistent with circle-bound NPCs lacking a basket, the two basket-associated proteins Esc1 and Ulp1 (both involved in telomeric silencing and mRNA surveillance; Bonnet et al., 2015) were excluded from NPC caps (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5A and B and citation to a previous study.

claim: None of the 10 importins tested were displaced from the NPC cap adjacent to DNA circle clusters.
source: In striking contrast, none of the 10 importins tested were displaced from the cap (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The exportins Xpo1 (Crm1), Msn5 and Los1 accumulated at the cap to similar extent as the core Nups.
source: Likewise, the exportins Xpo1 (Crm1), Msn5 and Los1, which ensure the export of proteins and tRNAs, accumulated at the cap to similar extent as the core Nups.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data.

claim: Basket-less pores interact with most transport factors with similar dynamics as bulk NPCs.
source: Since nearly all these proteins accumulated to the same extent as core NPCs in the cap compared to elsewhere in the nuclear envelope, we concluded that basket-less pores interact with them with similar dynamics as bulk NPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most transport factors accumulate similarly to core NPCs at the cap.

claim: Two importins, Srp1/Kap60 and Kap123, were significantly enriched in the cap compared to bulk NPCs.
source: However, two importins were significantly enriched in the cap compared to bulk NPCs, namely Srp1/Kap60 and Kap123.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data.

claim: Both Kap60 and Kap123 decayed with identical kinetics at the cap-NPCs as elsewhere in the nuclear envelope upon FLIP.
source: Quantification of the fluorescence signal showed that both proteins decayed with identical kinetics at the cap-NPCs as elsewhere in the nuclear envelope (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by FLIP data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Importins' interaction with circle-bound and circle-free NPCs followed undistinguishable kinetics.
source: Thus, importins' interaction with circle-bound and circle-free NPCs followed undistinguishable kinetics.
evidence: This is concluded from the FLIP experiments showing identical decay kinetics.

claim: The absence of the basket or the presence of an ERC increases the frequency with which Kap60 and Kap123 interact with NPCs but not the time they spend in them.
source: Somehow the absence of the basket or the presence of an ERC increases the frequency with which Kap60 and Kap123 interact with NPCs but not the time they spend in them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that these importins are enriched at the cap but show identical kinetics.

claim: Old cells accumulated the import reporter protein NLS-3xGFP in the nucleus at least as tightly as young cells.
source: Consistent with circle-bound NPCs being fully functional for nuclear import and not leaky (as already seen in Morlot et al., 2019; Rempel et al., 2019), old cells accumulated the import reporter protein NLS-3xGFP in the nucleus at least as tightly as young cells (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C-E and citations to previous studies.

claim: Old cells accumulate NLS-3xGFP more tightly in the nucleus than young ones.
source: In fact, the nucleo/cytoplasmic ratio of fluorescence show that old cells accumulate NLS-3xGFP more tightly in the nucleus than young ones (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The NPCs of old yeast cells, including ERC-associated NPCs, are fully functional in the nuclear import and retention of proteins.
source: We conclude that the NPCs of old yeast cells, including ERC-associated NPCs, are fully functional in the nuclear import and retention of proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from the NLS-3xGFP accumulation data.

claim: Five exportins involved in mRNA export were specifically depleted from cap NPCs.
source: Interestingly however, our quantifications indicated that 5 exportins were specifically depleted from cap NPCs (Figure 5B), indicating that the interaction of these proteins with core NPCs was substantially decreased. Interestingly, all these exportins are involved in mRNA export.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All seven proteins found to be excluded from the cap are involved in mRNA export.
source: Thus, all seven proteins that we find to be excluded from the cap are involved in this process (Bonnet et al., 2015; Iglesias et al., 2010; Stewart, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs are deprived of the TREX-2 complex, as judged by assaying the localization of its Sac3 subunit.
source: Consistent with the circle-bound NPCs being defective at mRNA export, they are also deprived of the TREX-2 complex, as judged by assaying the localization of its Sac3 subunit (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs show a very specific decrease in mRNA export activity and an increased capacity for protein import.
source: Together, these observations indicate that circle-bound NPCs are not fundamentally defective but may rather show a very specific decrease in mRNA export activity and an increased capacity for protein import.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective loss of mRNA export factors and enrichment of some importins.

claim: Three of the four basket proteins displaced from circle-bound NPCs are acetylated in vivo, at least in part through SAGA.
source: Indeed, three of the four basket proteins displaced from circle-bound NPCs are acetylated in vivo, at least in part through SAGA (Downey et al., 2015; Henriksen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nup60 is prominently acetylated on lysine 467 in a Gcn5-dependent manner.
source: Particularly, Nup60, which anchors the Mlp proteins to NPCs (Feuerbach et al., 2002) is prominently acetylated on lysine 467 in a Gcn5-dependent manner (Choudhary et al., 2009; Choudhary et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nup60-K467R accumulated in the cap nearly as much as core Nups.
source: Strikingly, not only did Nup60-K467R accumulate in the cap nearly as much as core Nups, but the localization of the cytoplasmic complexes (Nup116, Nup42, Gle1, and Gle2) to cap NPCs was also restored (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The localization of the cytoplasmic complexes (Nup116, Nup42, Gle1, and Gle2) to cap NPCs was restored in the Nup60-K467R mutant.
source: Strikingly, not only did Nup60-K467R accumulate in the cap nearly as much as core Nups, but the localization of the cytoplasmic complexes (Nup116, Nup42, Gle1, and Gle2) to cap NPCs was also restored (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: The basket protein Mlp1 remained displaced in the Nup60-K467R mutant.
source: In contrast, the basket protein Mlp1 remained displaced.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data.

claim: Acetylation of Nup60 on K467 upon circle attachment displaces it from NPCs and also subsequently dissociates the cytoplasmic complexes.
source: Thus, acetylation of Nup60 on K467 upon circle attachment displaces it from NPCs and somehow also subsequently dissociates the cytoplasmic complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that preventing Nup60 acetylation restores both Nup60 and cytoplasmic complexes to the cap.

claim: Nup60 acetylation alone explains the detachment of the rest of the basket since Nup60 mediates the anchorage of Mlps to NPCs.
source: Since Nup60 mediates the anchorage of Mlps to NPCs (Feuerbach et al., 2002), Nup60 acetylation alone explains the detachment of the rest of the basket.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of Nup60 and supported by citation.

claim: Additional events re-enforce the displacement of Mlp1/2 beyond Nup60 acetylation, possibly involving their own acetylation or that of Nup2.
source: However, our data indicate that additional events re-enforce the displacement of Mlp1/2, in addition to Nup60 acetylation. These events might involve their own acetylation or that of Nup2.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that Mlp1 remains displaced in the Nup60-K467R mutant.

claim: Wild type cells showed a replicative life span of 18 generations in the optimized microfluidic setup.
source: In this optimized setup, the wild type cells reproducibly showed a replicative life span of 18 generations (Figure 8C), well within the range of lifespans reported for wild-type cells measured on different microfluidic platforms (Chen et al., 2017; Janssens and Veenhoff, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 8C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutant cells lacking the central basket component Nup60 aged rapidly with a median life span of 13 divisions.
source: These measurements established that mutant cells lacking the central basket component Nup60 aged rapidly (median life span of 13 divisions).
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data.

claim: The nup60-K467R mutant cells showed a modest but significantly extended longevity of 20 divisions.
source: In reverse, the nup60-K467R mutant cells showed a modest but significantly extended longevity (20 divisions, Figure 8C), despite the proteins Mlp1 and Mlp2 still being displaced from NPCs.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Basket removal promotes ageing.
source: Thus, we conclude that basket removal promotes ageing and that stimulation of this process by ERCs and SAGA limits the longevity of yeast cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the lifespan data showing that preventing basket removal extends lifespan.

claim: Stimulation of basket removal by ERCs and SAGA limits the longevity of yeast cells.
source: Thus, we conclude that basket removal promotes ageing and that stimulation of this process by ERCs and SAGA limits the longevity of yeast cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data on ERC-dependent basket removal and lifespan extension in mutants.

claim: Circle anchorage to NPCs contributes to the mechanisms by which extrachromosomal DNA circles promote cellular ageing.
source: First, they not only confirm that ERCs and DNA circles in general attach to NPCs in ageing yeast cells, they establish that this in turn affects the organization and function of the NPCs retained in the mother cell. Thereby, anchorage to NPCs contributes to the mechanisms by which extrachromosomal DNA circles promote cellular ageing.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined data showing that circle attachment causes NPC remodeling and that preventing this remodeling extends lifespan.

claim: Circle-attachment to NPCs is a fundamental driver of ageing, at least in yeast.
source: Thus, circle-attachment to NPCs is a fundamental driver of ageing, at least in yeast.
evidence: This is concluded from the data showing that circle attachment drives NPC remodeling which promotes ageing.

claim: Circle anchorage does not damage NPCs but rather activates a regulatory process that involves the compositional and functional reorganization of NPCs.
source: Second, circle anchorage does not appear to damage NPCs but rather to activate a regulatory process that involves the compositional and functional reorganization of NPCs.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of ESCRT recruitment and the acetylation-dependent mechanism of basket removal.

claim: Circles might drive ageing through an imbalance in or overabundance of specialized NPCs.
source: Thus, circles might drive ageing through an imbalance in or overabundance of specialized NPCs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that circle-bound NPCs are specialized for protein import over mRNA export.

claim: The asymmetric partition of DNA circles during yeast mitosis involves their attachment to NPCs and subsequent confinement into the mother cell by a lateral diffusion barrier.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates that the asymmetric partition of DNA circles during yeast mitosis involves their attachment to NPCs and subsequent confinement into the mother cell by a lateral diffusion barrier (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Clay et al., 2014; Ouellet and Barral, 2012; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Abrogating the lateral diffusion barrier made of phytoceramide causes NPCs and DNA circles to leak to the bud, extending the mother cells lifespan.
source: Indeed, abrogating this barrier, made of phytoceramide (Clay et al., 2014; Megyeri et al., 2019; Prasad et al., 2020), causes NPCs and DNA circles to leak to the bud, extending the mother cells lifespan (Boettcher et al., 2012; Megyeri et al., 2019; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Releasing DNA circles from their anchorage to NPCs by SAGA extends mother cell lifespan.
source: Releasing DNA circles from their anchorage to NPCs by SAGA has the same effects (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; McCormick et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Artificially binding the basket proteins Nup2 or Mlp1 to DNA circles releases them from retention in the mother cell.
source: However, in apparent contradiction to this idea, previous studies have established that artificially binding the basket proteins Nup2 or Mlp1 (fused to TetR) to DNA circles releases them from retention in the mother cell (Khmelinskii et al., 2011), suggesting that tethering circles to NPCs bypasses rather than promotes their confinement in the mother cell.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Tethering circles to core Nups did not impair their retention in the mother cell and restored retention when the endogenous SAGA-dependent mechanism was abrogated.
source: Nevertheless, that study and a subsequent one (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014) also indicated that tethering circles to core Nups did not impair their retention in the mother cell. Rather, it restored their retention when the endogenous, SAGA-dependent mechanism of anchorage was abrogated.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA circles and the nuclear basket exclude each other at NPCs.
source: The absence of Mlp1 and Nup2 from circle-bound NPCs indicate that DNA circles and the nuclear basket exclude each other at NPCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that basket proteins are displaced from circle-bound NPCs.

claim: Decorating a model DNA circle with basket proteins may cause both circle and basket to detach from NPCs, explaining their random segregation between mother and bud.
source: Thus, decorating a model DNA circle with basket proteins may cause both circle and basket to detach rather than to dock to NPCs, explaining their random segregation between mother and bud.
evidence: This is speculated to explain the apparent contradiction in previous studies.

claim: The NPCs of old cells remain tight and promote the accumulation of nuclear proteins in the nucleus.
source: The NPCs of old yeast mother cells remain tight and promote the accumulation of nuclear proteins in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by the NLS-3xGFP accumulation data.

claim: The proper presence of Nup82 and Nup159 in circle-bound NPCs indicates that these NPCs must have originally contained Nup116, which they must have lost ulteriorly.
source: Indeed, Nup116 is essential for the recruitment of Nup82 and Nup159 to NPCs (Allegretti et al., 2020). Thus, the proper presence of Nup82 and Nup159 in circle-bound NPCs indicates that these NPCs must have originally contained Nup116, which they must have lost ulteriorly.
evidence: This is inferred from the known assembly requirements and supported by citation.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs must have lost their basket only during or after circle attachment since the basket is required for SAGA-dependent recruitment of chromatin to NPCs.
source: The same argument can be made for the basket. Indeed, the basket is required for SAGA-dependent recruitment of chromatin, including circles, to NPCs (Dieppois et al., 2006; Shcheprova et al., 2008; Texari et al., 2013). Therefore, circle-bound NPCs must have lost their basket only during or after circle attachment.
evidence: This is inferred from the known requirement of the basket for circle attachment and supported by citations.

claim: The allele Nup60-K467R stabilizes Nup116 on circle-bound NPCs, indicating that Nup116 is most probably released from NPCs after Nup60 acetylation upon circle docking.
source: Remarkably, the allele Nup60-K467R, which is not displaced from NPCs upon circle binding, stabilizes Nup116 on circle-bound NPCs, indicating that Nup116 is most probably released from NPCs after Nup60 acetylation, that is, upon circle docking (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that preventing Nup60 acetylation retains Nup116 at circle-bound NPCs.

claim: NPCs become extensively remodeled upon DNA circle attachment rather than being incomplete in the first place.
source: Thus, our data suggest that NPCs become extensively remodeled upon DNA circle attachment rather than being incomplete in the first place.
evidence: This is concluded from the evidence that circle-bound NPCs were properly assembled initially.

claim: All Nups lacking from old cells and circle-bound NPCs have been shown to turnover at NPCs by microscopy or mass-spectrometry methods.
source: Interestingly, all Nups lacking from old cells and circle-bound NPCs have been shown to turnover at NPCs by microscopy (Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014) or mass-spectrometry methods (Hakhverdyan et al., 2021): The basket components Nup2 and Nup60, and the cytoplasmic complex component Gle1 are highly mobile at NPCs. Nup116, Nup42, Gle2, Mlp1, and Mlp2 turnover a bit slower but are also mobile.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All core Nups which are stable at the NPC cap fail to show turnover by mass-spectrometry.
source: In contrast, all core Nups which are stable at the NPC cap fail to show turnover by mass-spectrometry.
evidence: This is supported by reference to mass-spectrometry data.

claim: Nup82 and Nup159 fail to show turnover by mass-spectrometry.
source: The same applies for Nup82 and Nup159, the NPC components on the cytoplasmic side that are not displaced from circle-bound NPCs (Hakhverdyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Nup1 and Nup53 are mobile but remain associated with circle-bound NPCs, indicating that circles do not displace all dynamic Nups, but only specific ones.
source: We noticed only two exceptions. Nup1 and Nup53 are mobile but remain associated with circle-bound NPCs (Hakhverdyan et al., 2021) indicating that circles do not displace all dynamic Nups, but only specific ones.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and the data showing these Nups remain at the cap.

claim: Circle-bound NPCs are not affected in their core; only the dynamics of specific mobile components seem to be changed.
source: Together, these data show that circle-bound NPCs are not affected in their core. Only the dynamics of specific mobile components seem to be changed.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that core Nups remain stable while only specific mobile Nups are displaced.

claim: SAGA promotes the docking of many genes to NPCs upon their activation in young cells.
source: In young cells, SAGA promotes the docking of many genes to NPCs upon their activation (Cabal et al., 2006; Huisinga and Pugh, 2004; Kremer and Gross, 2009; Luthra et al., 2007) and Nup60 acetylation controls the expression of diverse genes (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nup60 acetylation controls the expression of diverse genes.
source: In young cells, SAGA promotes the docking of many genes to NPCs upon their activation (Cabal et al., 2006; Huisinga and Pugh, 2004; Kremer and Gross, 2009; Luthra et al., 2007) and Nup60 acetylation controls the expression of diverse genes (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The residence of the basket at NPCs is dynamic in young cells.
source: The residence of the basket at NPCs is also dynamic in young cells (Akey et al., 2022; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Hakhverdyan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The acetylation-dependent removal of the basket in circle-bound NPCs reflects a regulatory event also frequent in young cells before circles are formed.
source: Thus, rather than a damage, the acetylation-dependent removal of the basket in circle-bound NPCs seems to reflect a regulatory event, also frequent in young cells, before circles are formed.
evidence: This is inferred from the dynamic nature of basket association and the acetylation-dependent mechanism.

claim: ERC attachment leads to the accumulation of too many specialized NPCs.
source: Thus, we suggest that ERC attachment leads to the accumulation of too many specialized NPCs.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that circle-bound NPCs are specialized and accumulate with age.

claim: The increased import of protein and possibly defective export of mRNAs may increase crowding in the nucleus and explain the misregulation of ribosome and nucleosome assembly observed in old cells.
source: Specifically, the increased import of protein and possibly a defective export of mRNAs (although the properly assembled NPCs remaining might be sufficient for this function) may increase crowding in the nucleus and explain the misregulation of ribosome and nucleosome assembly observe in old cells (Janssens et al., 2015; Morlot et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculated based on the functional changes in circle-bound NPCs and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In budding yeast, the NPCs adjacent to the nucleolus have no basket.
source: In budding yeast, the NPCs adjacent to the nucleolus have no basket (Galy et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2004) and all yeast NPCs lose their basket in response to heat stress (Carmody et al., 2010), documenting that basket removal is indeed a recurrent mode of NPC regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All yeast NPCs lose their basket in response to heat stress.
source: In budding yeast, the NPCs adjacent to the nucleolus have no basket (Galy et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2004) and all yeast NPCs lose their basket in response to heat stress (Carmody et al., 2010), documenting that basket removal is indeed a recurrent mode of NPC regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Basket removal is a recurrent mode of NPC regulation.
source: In budding yeast, the NPCs adjacent to the nucleolus have no basket (Galy et al., 2004; Zhao et al., 2004) and all yeast NPCs lose their basket in response to heat stress (Carmody et al., 2010), documenting that basket removal is indeed a recurrent mode of NPC regulation.
evidence: This is concluded from the examples of basket removal in different contexts.

claim: Progerin, a progeriatric isoform of Lamin A causing Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome in humans, displaces Nup153 and TPR from the nuclear periphery.
source: Most remarkably, progerin, a progeriatric isoform of Lamin A and causing the Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome in humans, displaces Nup153 and TPR (the mammalian homologs of Nup60 and Mlp1/2) from the nuclear periphery (Balmus et al., 2018; Cobb et al., 2016; Kelley et al., 2011; Larrieu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The effects of ageing on NPCs and the role of NPCs in ageing might be strikingly similar between yeast and mammals.
source: Thus, the effects of ageing on NPCs and the role of NPCs in ageing might be strikingly similar between yeast and mammals.
evidence: This is speculated based on the similarity between progerin effects and ERC-induced NPC changes.

claim: The antagonistic pleiotropy theory suggests that ageing emerges upon fixation of traits and processes that have selective advantage early in life, despite being deleterious later-on.
source: This theory suggests that ageing emerges upon fixation of traits and processes that have selective advantage early in life, despite being deleterious later-on.
evidence: This is established knowledge about evolutionary theory of ageing.

claim: The ability to restructure and specialize NPCs plays an important role in how cells adapt to a variety of stresses and environmental changes.
source: The data available suggest that the ability to restructure and specialize NPCs plays an important role in how cells adapt to a variety of stresses and environmental changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the examples of NPC remodeling in different contexts.

claim: The essential function of NPC restructuring and specialization happens at the cost of longevity.
source: Our data suggest that this essential function happens at the cost of longevity.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that NPC remodeling promotes ageing.
